0.title: Hope at the Last Enemy
0.essay:
Death is the one certainty of human life. Our culture does its best not to think about it. Scripture speaks about it honestly and often, and with a hope that changes everything.

A culture that looks away

People today often die in hospitals rather than at home. Funerals are short, and conversation about death is considered morbid. Yet everyone will face it: the death of those they love, and their own.

Enemy and defeated foe

Scripture does not soften death. It is an enemy, the wages of sin, a terrible intrusion into God’s good world. And yet, for those in Christ, death has lost its sting. Jesus said, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live” (John 11:25). The Christian faces death not with denial or despair, but with sober realism and living hope.

A pastoral study

This study is pastoral. It is not mainly about debates over the order of end-time events, which the End Times study covers. It asks practical and personal questions. Why do we die? How did Christ conquer death? How can we prepare to die well? How should Christians grieve? What happens when we die? And what is heaven really like?

The chapters

The Last Enemy; Christ Has Conquered Death; Preparing to Die Well; Grieving with Hope; What Happens When We Die?; and The New Heavens and the New Earth.

For reflection

When did you last think seriously about your own death? What feelings rise when you do?

1.title: The Last Enemy
1.essay:
Death was not part of God’s original creation. It is an intruder, the consequence of sin, and Scripture calls it an enemy.

Not how it was meant to be

God made a world that was “very good” (Genesis 1:31). He warned Adam about the forbidden tree: “in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die” (Genesis 2:17). When Adam sinned, the sentence fell: “for you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). Every funeral echoes those words.

So death is not “natural” in the sense of being what God intended. It is an intruder. But in the very chapter where death enters, God promised an offspring of the woman who would crush the serpent (Genesis 3:15). The curse is not the end of the story.

The result of sin

“Therefore, just as sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men because all sinned” (Romans 5:12). “For the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23).

This does not mean every individual death is punishment for a particular sin. Babies die, and righteous people die young. But death as such is the consequence of humanity’s rebellion against God. And Paul at once sets Adam beside Christ: “much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:17). Death came through a man; life comes through a man.

An enemy

“The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26). Christians should not pretend death is beautiful, or simply a natural part of life. When Jesus stood at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, “he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled” (John 11:33), and he wept. He grieved, and was angered, at death’s destruction, even though he was about to raise Lazarus.

Three kinds of death

Scripture speaks of death in more than one sense. Spiritual death is separation from God, the state of all people by nature: “you were dead in the trespasses and sins” (Ephesians 2:1). Physical death is the separation of soul from body. And eternal death, “the second death” (Revelation 20:14), is final separation from God’s favour. Christ saves from all three.

Certain and soon

“It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Hebrews 9:27). And life is short: “The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty; yet their span is but toil and trouble; they are soon gone, and we fly away” (Psalm 90:10). We do not know when death will come.

Number our days

The right response is not denial but prayer: “So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom” (Psalm 90:12). Counting our days is not morbid. It is the beginning of wisdom. Remembering our mortality makes us humble, focused and ready.

The Preacher puts it more sharply: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart” (Ecclesiastes 7:2). Funerals remind us of what really matters. Sorrow can make the heart wise. Fools avoid the subject; the wise lay it to heart.

Think of a busy professional who has never thought seriously about death. Then a colleague her own age dies suddenly. At the funeral she realises how fragile life is, and begins to read the Bible again, asking what really lasts. The house of mourning taught her what the house of feasting never did.

The fear of death

Hebrews speaks of “those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:15). Much human anxiety, ambition and distraction is driven by a hidden fear of death. Facing death honestly, in the light of the gospel, brings freedom.

And he died

Genesis 5 traces the line from Adam to Noah with a sombre refrain: “and he died.” Name after name, the same ending. But one man breaks the pattern: “Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him” (Genesis 5:24). Even in the shadow of death, God gave a hint that death would not have the last word.

For reflection

If you knew you would die this year, what would you change about how you are living? What has a funeral, or the death of someone close, taught you?

2.title: Christ Has Conquered Death
2.essay:
The heart of the Christian hope is not that death is unreal, but that Christ has defeated it.

He died our death

The Son of God took on flesh and blood “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:14–15). He became human so that he could die. He entered death itself, bearing the penalty for sin. Because he has paid for sin, death no longer has a legal claim on those who belong to him.

He rose

On the third day Jesus walked out of the tomb. He was not merely resuscitated, to die again later. He was raised to immortal, glorified life. “We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him” (Romans 6:9). His resurrection is the firstfruits of the harvest to come. Paul says that Christ “abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2 Timothy 1:10). Death’s final removal awaits his return, but its defeat is already accomplished.

He holds the keys

When John saw the glorified Christ, he fell at his feet as though dead. Jesus laid his hand on him and said, “Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:17–18).

Death is not in charge. Christ is. No believer will pass through the door of death except when he opens it, and he will be on the other side.

Death has lost its sting

“O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting? The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:55–57). For the believer, death is like a bee that has lost its sting. It can still frighten and hurt, but it cannot destroy. Its poison was drained into Christ.

And Paul draws a practical conclusion: “Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58). The resurrection gives eternal meaning to ordinary faithfulness.

A doorway

For Christians, death is no longer an end but a passage into Christ’s presence. Paul could say, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). Jesus spoke of a believer’s death as sleep: “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him” (John 11:11). Not because the dead become unconscious, but because they will wake again.

I am the resurrection

At Lazarus’s tomb, Martha said she knew her brother would rise on the last day. Jesus pointed her to himself: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?” (John 11:25–26). Everything depends on the answer.

Then he called, “Lazarus, come out” (John 11:43), and the dead man came out. The resurrection is not only a doctrine. It is a person, and he has power over the grave.

The body too

The Christian hope is not only that the soul goes to heaven, but that the body will be raised. Christ’s resurrection is the pattern: the same body, transformed and glorified. God will not abandon the bodies he made. Believers die in Christ, and even in the grave they remain united to him; they are “the dead in Christ” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). Nothing, not even death, can separate us from his love (Romans 8:38–39).

Waiting on the other side

Think of an elderly Christian man told by his doctor that he has weeks to live. He is surprisingly calm. His grandson asks if he is afraid. He answers, “I’m not looking forward to the dying. But I’m not afraid of death. Jesus has been through it ahead of me, and he’s waiting on the other side.”

For reflection

Do you fear death? Bring that fear to the risen Christ, who holds the keys. How does 1 Corinthians 15:58 connect the resurrection to your everyday life?

3.title: Preparing to Die Well
3.essay:
In earlier centuries Christians wrote books on the art of dying well. They believed that preparing for death was part of a faithful life. Scripture encourages us to be ready.

Ready spiritually

The most important preparation is to be right with God through faith in Christ. Jesus told of a rich man whose harvest was so great that he planned bigger barns and a life of ease. “But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you’” (Luke 12:20). His problem was not his wealth, but that he planned his life as if death would never come. “So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God” (Luke 12:21). No one should put off repentance and faith, assuming there will be time later.

Ready relationally

Death often reveals unfinished business: unforgiven wrongs, words left unsaid, broken relationships. While there is time, seek reconciliation, ask forgiveness, express love and gratitude, and bless those you will leave behind.

Before he died, Jacob gathered his sons and blessed each of them (Genesis 49). Joseph made his brothers promise to carry his bones to the promised land (Genesis 50:24–25). These men died looking forward to God’s promises. “These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar” (Hebrews 11:13).

Ready practically

Caring for one’s family includes practical preparation: making a will, arranging finances, discussing medical wishes and funeral plans. These are acts of love that spare a grieving family confusion and conflict. “But if anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith” (1 Timothy 5:8).

Think of a Christian woman diagnosed with a terminal illness who uses her remaining months well. She makes a will, and plans her funeral with her pastor, choosing hymns of hope. She writes letters to her children and grandchildren, telling them how much she loves them and urging them to trust Christ. She is reconciled with an estranged sister. When she dies, her family grieves deeply, but they have been given a gift.

Finish well

Paul, facing execution, wrote, “For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:6–7). He did not look back on a perfect life, but a faithful one. And he looked forward to “the crown of righteousness,” which the Lord will give “not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing” (2 Timothy 4:8). Paul died well because he had lived well.

Longing, but not impatience

Writing from prison, not knowing whether he would live or die, Paul said, “My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account” (Philippians 1:23–24). A Christian can hold both: a desire to be with Christ, and a willingness to keep serving for as long as God wills.

Strangers seeking a better country

The patriarchs knew they were strangers and exiles on earth. “But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city” (Hebrews 11:16).

End-of-life decisions

Life is God’s gift, and deliberately ending it is forbidden (Exodus 20:13). That rules out euthanasia and assisted suicide, even when motivated by compassion. But Christians are not required to accept every possible treatment. It is right to decline treatments that are burdensome and offer little hope, and to accept good pain relief, even if it may shorten life as a side effect. The line is between allowing death and causing it. The Life Ethics study explores this further.

Suicide

Taking one’s own life is a grave sin. But it is not the unforgivable sin. A true believer who dies this way, in despair or illness of mind, is not cut off from the grace that saves sinners, for salvation rests on Christ’s work, not on the state of our last moment (Romans 8:38–39). Anyone thinking of it should speak to someone today: a pastor, a friend, a doctor, or a crisis line.

Deathbed conversions

The thief on the cross shows that it is never too late to turn to Christ. He said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom,” and Jesus promised him paradise that very day (Luke 23:42–43). But it is dangerous to presume on it. Many die suddenly, and hearts harden over time.

For reflection

If you died tomorrow, what would you leave undone? Is there a relationship to put right, or a practical step to take, this week?

4.title: Grieving with Hope
4.essay:
Christians grieve. Faith does not remove sorrow, and pretending to feel none is not spiritual maturity. But Christians grieve differently: with hope.

The saints wept

Abraham wept for Sarah (Genesis 23:2). David wept for Absalom (2 Samuel 18:33). “Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him” (Acts 8:2). And Jesus wept for Lazarus.

When Mary fell at his feet and said, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (John 11:32), he did not rebuke her honest grief. He was deeply moved, asked where Lazarus was laid, and wept. The onlookers said, “See how he loved him!” (John 11:36). He knew he was about to raise Lazarus, and still he wept at death’s cruelty. Jesus’ tears dignify ours. He weeps with us.

Not as those without hope

“But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The Thessalonians feared that believers who died before Christ’s return had missed out. Paul assures them that the dead in Christ will rise first, and all believers will be together with the Lord. “Therefore encourage one another with these words” (1 Thessalonians 4:18).

Notice: Paul does not say “do not grieve.” He says grieve differently. Christian grief is real, sometimes deep and long. But it is grief with a horizon. We will see our loved ones in Christ again.

Think of a widower in his sixties who feels guilty for still grieving his wife a year after her death. People at church seem to expect him to have moved on. A friend reads him 1 Thessalonians 4:13 and says, “Paul doesn’t tell you not to grieve. He tells you to grieve with hope. Take all the time you need.” The widower weeps, and feels lighter.

God is near

“The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit” (Psalm 34:18). Grieving people often feel God is far away. Scripture assures them he is closest when they are most broken. That does not mean the righteous escape affliction: “Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all” (Psalm 34:19). He is near in the meantime. The psalms of lament give words for grief: anger, confusion, exhaustion and longing.

Grief takes time

There is no timetable for grief. Waves of sorrow may return on anniversaries, at Christmas, or unexpectedly at the sound of a song. That is normal. Grief is the cost of love.

Comforting the grieving

The church is called to “weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). Job’s friends did best in the first week, when they sat with him in silence (Job 2:13). The most helpful comfort is often presence, not explanations. Practical help — meals, childcare, help with paperwork — is a gift. And remembering the bereaved months later, when others have moved on, is a great kindness.

I shall go to him

David fasted and wept while his infant son was ill. When the child died, he rose, washed and worshipped. His servants were puzzled. He explained, “But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me” (2 Samuel 12:23). Grieving parents have taken comfort in those words for centuries.

Do infants who die go to be with the Lord? Scripture does not set out a full doctrine, and Christians have answered differently. But God is merciful, and Jesus welcomed little children: “Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:14). Many in the Reformed tradition have held that God saves those who die in infancy, by his grace in Christ. Grieving parents may rest their little ones in God’s hands with real hope.

Will we know each other?

Scripture suggests we will. David expected to be with his son. Moses and Elijah were recognisable at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3). Paul expected to rejoice over the Thessalonians at Christ’s coming (1 Thessalonians 2:19). Relationships will be transformed, not erased.

When the dead were not believers

This is one of the hardest griefs. We cannot know what passed between a person and God in their final moments. We can leave them in the hands of the One of whom Abraham asked, “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25), and trust that his justice and mercy are perfect.

Some grief is complicated by suicide, violence, estrangement or a difficult relationship. Such grief may need extra care and wise counsel. The Biblical Counseling study has a chapter on grief and loss.

For reflection

Who do you know who is grieving? How could you comfort them this week without offering empty answers?

5.title: What Happens When We Die?
5.essay:
What happens to a believer between death and the resurrection? Scripture does not tell us everything, but it tells us enough.

Today

Two criminals were crucified beside Jesus. One mocked him. The other rebuked him, admitted his own guilt, and asked Jesus to remember him. Jesus promised more than he asked: “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Not someday, but today. No baptism, no good works, no time to make amends. Just faith in the dying King, and the promise of paradise that very day.

At home with the Lord

Paul writes, “we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8). He longed “to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better” (Philippians 1:23). He was not weary of life or trying to escape responsibility. He simply knew where he would be. For the believer, death is not a long sleep in nothingness, but immediate entrance into Christ’s presence.

As Stephen was being stoned, he said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:56). And he prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59). He knew where he was going, and who would receive him.

Conscious and at rest

The souls of believers are conscious after death. In Revelation, John sees the souls of martyrs under the heavenly altar. They speak, asking God how long until he brings justice, and they are given white robes and told to rest a little longer (Revelation 6:9–11). The Spirit says of those who die in the Lord, “that they may rest from their labors” (Revelation 14:13). This is often called the intermediate state: a real, conscious, blessed existence with Christ while awaiting the resurrection.

Think of a young mother terrified that when she dies she will simply cease to exist, or lie unconscious for centuries. Reading Luke 23:43 and Philippians 1:23, she finds great comfort. She will be with Christ, immediately and consciously. Her fear does not vanish overnight, but it loses its grip.

Not yet complete

The intermediate state is not the final goal. Believers who have died are with Christ, but still waiting for the resurrection of their bodies and the renewal of all things. Paul describes the soul without the body as being “unclothed,” and says he does not long for that for its own sake, but to be “further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Corinthians 5:4). Our hope is not merely to escape the body, but to receive it back, glorified. The best is yet to come.

The unbelieving dead

Jesus’ story of the rich man and Lazarus describes the rich man after death in torment, conscious and aware, with Abraham saying, “between us and you a great chasm has been fixed” (Luke 16:26). Death fixes a person’s destiny. There is no second chance afterwards: “it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment” (Hebrews 9:27).

The views

Some teach “soul sleep”: that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. The Roman Catholic Church teaches purgatory, a place of purifying suffering for many believers before they enter heaven. Others hold that believers go immediately and consciously into Christ’s presence.

The last view is right. Jesus’ promise of “today,” Paul’s “far better,” and the conscious souls in Revelation 6 rule out soul sleep. And purgatory has no basis in Scripture. It contradicts the sufficiency of Christ’s sacrifice: “For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). Nothing remains to be paid.

Praying for the dead

Since the destiny of the dead is fixed, Scripture gives no command or example of praying for the dead. We pray for the living, and we thank God for those who have died in faith.

Near-death experiences

Christians should be cautious about building beliefs on reported experiences of heaven or hell. Scripture, not experience, is our guide to what lies beyond death.

For reflection

When you think of a believing loved one who has died, do you picture them as gone, or as with Christ? What does Jesus’ word “today” mean for you?

6.title: The New Heavens and the New Earth
6.essay:
Many Christians imagine heaven as an endless church service in the clouds, with souls floating on harps. The Bible’s picture is far richer and more solid. The final hope is not that we leave the earth for heaven, but that heaven and earth are made new and joined for ever.

A renewed creation

“Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away” (Revelation 21:1). Paul says “the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 8:21). Peter writes, “according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3:13). God will not throw away his creation. He will renew it.

Some think the present world will be completely destroyed and replaced. More likely, Scripture teaches renewal through purifying judgment, as the flood purged but did not annihilate the world (2 Peter 3:6–7). There is continuity as well as transformation, just as Christ’s resurrection body was the same body, glorified.

Groaning towards birth

Paul says present sufferings “are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us” (Romans 8:18). Creation itself groans like a woman in labour, and believers groan too, waiting for the redemption of their bodies. The pain is real, but it is the pain of birth, not of death.

God with us

“Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3). The goal of the whole Bible is fulfilled: God living with his people. And at the centre of it all is the Lamb.

No more tears

“He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21:4). Every grief, disease, injustice and sin will be gone. Every wrong will be put right. And the one on the throne says, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5). It is the final chapter of the Bible’s story, and the beginning of an endless one.

Resurrection bodies

Believers will live in real, physical bodies. Paul uses the image of a seed: “What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power” (1 Corinthians 15:42–43). Christ “will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body” (Philippians 3:21). “Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:49).

The disabled will run. The aged will be young. The broken will be whole. Think of a young man with a severe disability who has never walked. Reading 1 Corinthians 15 and Revelation 21, he realises his body will be raised whole. He tells his pastor, “The first thing I’m going to do is run to Jesus.” That hope is not escapism. It gives him strength for the hard days now.

The garden become a city

The river of life flows from the throne, and the tree of life, lost in Eden, is restored: “The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations” (Revelation 22:2). “No longer will there be anything accursed, but the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face” (Revelation 22:3–4). The Bible ends where it began, in a garden with God, but now the garden has become a city full of the redeemed.

What will we do?

Scripture hints at a life full of meaning. We will worship God and see his face. We “will reign forever and ever” (Revelation 22:5). “They will bring into it the glory and the honor of the nations” (Revelation 21:26). There will be feasting: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). It will not be boring. It will be life as it was always meant to be, without sin, for ever.

One return, one new creation

Isaiah’s vision of “new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17), with long lives and the wolf and the lamb feeding together, is best read as a picture of the new creation in the language of the Old Testament world, rather than of a future earthly thousand-year reign. Christ will return once, raise the dead, and bring in the eternal state.

Marriage fulfilled

Jesus said that in the resurrection people “neither marry nor are given in marriage” (Matthew 22:30). That is not a loss. Human marriage points to the marriage of Christ and his church, and in the new creation the reality will have come.

Who will be there?

“But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life” (Revelation 21:27). And the invitation is open now: “And let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price” (Revelation 22:17).

John received this vision in exile on Patmos, in a world where Christians were persecuted and dying. He saw the end of the story: God wiping away every tear. That vision has sustained the church through centuries of suffering.

For reflection

When you think of eternity, do you think of something vague and cloudy, or solid and joyful? Read Revelation 21–22 this week, and let Scripture shape your hope.
